title: The health-probe interval is a per-environment durable setting the scheduler honours
description: Split from task-6ec875f4 DoD 5 by governor ruling (20:10Z), on worker-f78e0703's measured finding (16:48Z): composition:579 registers ONE monitoring/health-probes job at the default 60 s and re-registers it at boot, ring.ts:223 probes every environment per tick, the options carry no interval map; child task-cc05c473 is DONE with 'default 60 s only' and is NOT reopened. Per-environment intervals are therefore not a production setting today; this row adds the setting. task-6ec875f4 certifies the shipped default-interval behaviour only.
definitionOfDone: An operator command writes a per-environment probe interval as a durable record (bounded: min/max asserted; refusal code + layer for out-of-range or unknown environment), read through a store port; default 60 s when unset.

The scheduler honours it: two environments with different intervals are probed at their own rates in a fake-clock test (assert probe counts per environment over a window), and a change takes effect without a daemon restart.
Boot re-registration honours the stored intervals - no overwrite back to the default and no double schedule after restart (probe RATE equal before/after, per environment).
The existing health read (`/deployments/health/read` once task-509c6c16 lands, else the current read) discloses the effective interval per environment and the browser exact decoder preserves it.
Fresh focused daemon tests + typecheck with nonzero counts; named broader gates disclosed per lease rules (`full-suite-gate`); physical .js bridges for any new runtime module.

SURFACE: a store port that reads and writes a per-environment interval, and resolves the EFFECTIVE value — the stored one when set, 60000 when unset. Keep the default in ONE place and export it; both the scheduler (step 4) and child task-620fb461's read will consume it, so a second copy would be a second source of truth.

BOUNDS AND REFUSALS ARE THIS ROW'S TO DEFINE and must be TIGHTER than the scheduler's `validInterval` (integer, >0, <=2_147_483_647 at durable-schedule.ts:32). Choose a defensible operational min and max (a probe interval below a few seconds is a self-inflicted load generator; above an hour it is not monitoring), state the reasoning in a comment at the site, and refuse out-of-range and unknown-environment each with a STABLE CODE AND A ROSTERED LAYER.

Do NOT widen `ScheduleCode` (durable-schedule.ts:16-18) and do NOT introduce a new `*_LAYER` constant — the scheduler's closed union is about scheduling faults; a bad interval is this module's fault. Validate the environment against the same admission the deployment side uses (`admitEnvironmentName`) rather than a fresh regex, so the two cannot drift.

Keep the module under the 250-line target.
implementationPlan.note:
Durable interval record landed: `probe-interval-record.ts` (119 lines, under the 250 target) + its one-line bridge `probe-interval-record.js` containing exactly `export * from "./probe-interval-record.ts";`, byte-matching the `health-probe-contracts.js` convention.

SURFACE. `createProbeIntervalRecord({store, projectId, now?})` returns `{read, write, stored}`. `read(env)` resolves the EFFECTIVE value - stored when set, `DEFAULT_PROBE_INTERVAL_MS` when unset. `stored()` returns only environments carrying a stored value (an unset environment is ABSENT, not 60000) - that distinction is what step 5 needs to decide which environments get a dedicated job. Durable as events `moe.probe-interval.set` on aggregate `probe-interval/<projectId>`, replayed last-write-wins, so a rewrite replaces rather than accumulates.

ONE SOURCE OF TRUTH. `DEFAULT_PROBE_INTERVAL_MS = 60_000` is exported here and consumed by the scheduler wiring and by child task-620fb461's read; no second literal.

BOUNDS, tighter than the scheduler's `validInterval` as required: `MIN_PROBE_INTERVAL_MS = 5_000`, `MAX_PROBE_INTERVAL_MS = 3_600_000`, both INCLUSIVE, reasoning stated in a comment at the site (below 5 s a probe is a load generator against the thing it watches; above an hour the signal outlives the outage). `admitProbeInterval` rejects NaN, Infinity, negatives, zero and non-integers before either bound is consulted.

REFUSALS - own codes, rostered layer, nothing widened. `PROBE_INTERVAL_OUT_OF_RANGE`, `PROBE_INTERVAL_ENVIRONMENT_INVALID`, `PROBE_INTERVAL_STORE_FAILED`, each `layer: "DAEMON_INGRESS"`. `ScheduleCode` untouched; no new `*_LAYER` constant. The codes are DISJOINT from the scheduler's `SCHEDULE_INPUT_INVALID`, so a step-3 arm asserting them cannot be silently satisfied by the scheduler answering first. Environment is admitted through the deployment side's own `admitEnvironmentName`, not a fresh regex. `write` checks environment BEFORE interval, deliberately.

FAIL-CLOSED REPLAY: a stored record that no longer admits deletes that environment's entry, so it falls back to the DEFAULT rate rather than to an unparsed or unbounded one.

implementationPlan.description:

ARMS:
(a) An unset environment resolves to the 60000 default — assert against the exported constant, not a retyped literal.
(b) A written interval reads back by value, and a SECOND environment's value is independent (write two, read both) — a single-environment arm passes against a store that keeps one global value.
(c) Below-min and above-max each refuse with their code AND layer. Include the exact boundary values on both sides: min-1 refuses, min is accepted, max is accepted, max+1 refuses. An off-by-one at a bound is the defect this arm exists to catch.

(e) An unknown / malformed environment name refuses with its own code AND layer.
(f) A rewrite replaces rather than accumulates — write, rewrite, read back the second value.

For the two NEW files, `git status --porcelain` them first and prove restoration by SHA256 against a %TEMP% backup in a SEPARATE call — `git diff` is blind to untracked paths and would certify nothing.

implementationPlan.note:
Two edits, no new scheduler, `+35/-4` total.

`health-probe-contracts.ts` (42 -> 57 lines): `healthProbeJobId(environment)` derives `monitoring/health-probes/<env>` FROM `HEALTH_PROBE_JOB_ID`, so a rename of one cannot leave the other behind, and `healthProbeJobEnvironment(id)` is its inverse for boot restore. - `createEnvironmentHealthProbeJob(options, environment)` probes exactly the environment it was built for and does not enumerate the ledger; an environment with no receipt still refuses PROBE_RECEIPT_MISSING down the same path.

implementationPlan.description:
COMPOSITION: REGISTER PER ENVIRONMENT AND STOP THE BOOT OVERWRITE (DoD 3). In `apps/daemon/src/daemon-store-foundation-composition.ts`, around `:632` / `:670` / `:672`.

THE DEFECT, restated so it is not 'fixed' vacuously: `:672` calls `schedules.register(HEALTH_PROBE_JOB_ID, healthProbe)` with no interval, so it takes `DEFAULT_SCHEDULE_INTERVAL_MS`, and `register` at `durable-schedule.ts:93` then persists that default OVER any stored value — every boot resets an operator's 30 s back to 60 s.

TWO CHANGES:
1. The resolver at `:670` currently answers only `id === HEALTH_PROBE_JOB_ID`. Make it resolve a per-environment id to that environment's job, so `restore()` can re-arm persisted ids after a restart. An unresolvable id already refuses `SCHEDULE_TARGET_UNRESOLVED` and is dropped (`:139-141`) — keep that behaviour for genuinely unknown ids rather than manufacturing a callback.
2. Register each environment at its EFFECTIVE interval read from the step-2 port — read the stored value FIRST and pass it, so the persisted value is re-persisted unchanged rather than clobbered. An environment with no stored interval registers at the 60000 default, which is correct and must stay correct.

Boot ORDER matters: if composition registers before reading the record, the default is already persisted and the read is too late. State the order in a comment at the site.

An environment appearing for the first time between boots must still get a schedule at the default — do not make registration conditional on a stored record existing.
implementationPlan.note:
Composition wired, +45 lines (725 -> 770; the file was already over the cap before this row and stays disclosed, not worsened structurally - the additions are three small blocks, not a new responsibility).

1. RESOLVER. `resolveProbe(id)` answers `HEALTH_PROBE_JOB_ID` with the sweep, and a per-environment id with a fresh `createEnvironmentHealthProbeJob` - but ONLY while that environment still has a stored interval. A persisted id whose record has since been cleared resolves to null ON PURPOSE, so `durable-schedule.ts:139-141` refuses SCHEDULE_TARGET_UNRESOLVED and drops the arm, and the sweep reclaims the environment at the default rate. Manufacturing a callback there would leave a second job probing at a rate no operator can still see - which is the orphan hazard the plan's step-7 adversarial list asks about, answered in production rather than in a note. `config.schedule?.resolve` is still chained for every other id.

2. REGISTRATION, ORDER FIRST. `probeIntervals.stored()` is read BEFORE any `register` call, and the reason is stated in a comment at the site: `durable-schedule.ts:93` persists whenever the incoming interval differs from the stored one, so registering first writes the default over the operator's value and a read afterwards only sees the default it just clobbered. That is exactly the vacuous "fix" risks item 1 warns about. The sweep is ALWAYS registered - at `DEFAULT_PROBE_INTERVAL_MS`, the record's own default, so there is still one source of truth - which keeps an environment appearing for the first time between boots probed at 60 s rather than not at all. Each stored environment is then registered at ITS value, so `:93`'s `!==` is false and nothing re-persists. Registration failure still closes and throws `CODE@LAYER`, now per id.

3. SWEEP EXCLUSION. `createHealthProbeJob(probeOptions, dedicated)` where `dedicated()` re-reads the durable record on every call rather than capturing it once. That is what makes a change take effect on the next tick instead of the next restart, and it is what stops an environment with its own job ALSO being swept - a genuine double schedule. A store that cannot answer yields the EMPTY set, so every environment falls back to the sweep at the default rate; failing closed here means more probing, never none.

NO LEAK ADDED. `createHealthProbeRing` is documented and measured as per-operation connections owning no shutdown handle (health-probe-ring.ts:90-93, `access()` closes in `finally`), so building a ring per resolved job holds nothing open. Teardown is still `schedules.release()` inside the single `close`.

It is GREEN and UNEDITED - `git diff --stat` on it is empty. The plan's literal design would have reddened it; this one does not.

implementationPlan.description:
THE FAKE-CLOCK SCHEDULER TEST (DoD 2 and DoD 3) in a new `apps/daemon/src/monitoring/health-probe-schedule.test.ts`. Inject `ScheduleConfig.timer` (durable-schedule.ts:9-15) — a `ScheduleTimer` whose `set(tick, intervalMs)` records the id's armed interval and hands back a handle you drive manually, and whose `clear(handle)` records the release. `now` is injectable too. No real timers, no wall-clock waiting.

ARMS:
(a) DIFFERENT RATES: two environments with different stored intervals, driven over the same window, are probed at their OWN rates — assert PROBE COUNTS PER ENVIRONMENT, not merely the intervals the timer was asked for. `set()`'s argument proves what was requested; the DoD asks what actually happened. A one-environment version of this arm is vacuous.
(b) A CHANGE TAKES EFFECT WITHOUT A RESTART: write a new interval through the port, re-register, and assert the environment's probe count over the next window follows the NEW rate while the other environment's is unchanged.
(c) BOOT RE-REGISTRATION, the defect from step 1: record each environment's armed interval and the persisted record, simulate the boot path, and assert the stored interval is BYTE-UNCHANGED and the rate is EQUAL before and after — per environment. This is the arm that was red in step 1.
(d) NO DOUBLE SCHEDULE: after a restart, exactly one live handle exists per environment. Assert from the timer's own ledger of `set` minus `clear`, not from a count of registrations.
(e) A NEWLY APPEARED environment with no stored record is scheduled at the 60000 default.

TEARDOWN (DoD 5, epic rail 4): release the schedule in a `finally` and assert the injected timer's `clear` was called for EVERY handle it created — a leaked interval makes every later gate on this board inadmissible. Assert it; do not assume it.

DRILL (c) and (a): revert the composition fix and confirm (c) reds; make both environments share one job id and confirm (a) reds. Restore each and prove it.
implementationPlan.note:
`health-probe-schedule.test.ts` added: 5 arms, `Test Files 1 passed (1)` / `Tests 5 passed (5)` EXIT 0, driven through the REAL `createStoreDependencies` with an injected `ScheduleTimer` and a fake HTTP port - no real timers, no wall-clock waiting, nothing reimplemented.

ARMS, against the plan's roster:
(a) DIFFERENT RATES: staging 10 s and production 20 s over one 60 s window -> probe COUNTS 6 and 3, counted per environment at the HTTP port by receipt URL. The armed intervals are also asserted, but the counts are what carry the clause - `set()`'s argument only proves what was requested.
(b) CHANGE WITHOUT RESTART: the interval is rewritten through the record while the SAME provider keeps running; the next sweep re-arms staging at 30 s; the following full window shows staging halved to 2 while production is untouched at 3. Production at 20 s (not 30 s) exists so the two rates cannot be confused after the change.
(c) BOOT RE-REGISTRATION: registrations byte-compared across a real close/reopen (`toEqual(before.registered)` on the whole event list, plus exact single-entry equality for `healthProbeJobId("staging") = 10000` and `HEALTH_PROBE_JOB_ID = 60000`), armed intervals equal, and the per-environment RATE equal - the second window matches the first exactly (6/3 -> 12/6).
(d) NO DOUBLE SCHEDULE: `timer.live()` is empty between shutdown and reboot, and `liveIntervals()` after the reboot equals the pre-shutdown set. Measured from the timer's own set-minus-clear ledger.
(e) NEWLY APPEARED ENVIRONMENT: `preview` is deployed BETWEEN boots with no stored interval; no new arm appears, and it is probed once per 60 s window by the sweep.
Plus one beyond the roster: a cleared interval record hands the environment back to the sweep with no double probe (6 dedicated + 1 sweep = 7, not 13).

TEARDOWN ASSERTED, NOT ASSUMED (epic rail 4): `withDaemon`'s `finally` closes the provider and then asserts `timer.arms.filter(arm => !arm.cleared)` is EMPTY - every handle the timer ever created has been released, including the genesis boot's.

PRODUCTION AMENDED IN THIS STEP, because writing arm (b) proved step 5 could not satisfy it.
